subject: Anatomy
summary: The brachial artery is the main arterial conduit of the upper arm, supplying the arm and forearm. It is a key landmark for blood pressure measurement and for vascular access in emergencies.

sections.p: The brachial artery continues the axillary artery at the inferior border of the teres major and ends at the elbow where it bifurcates into the radial and ulnar arteries.
b: Major conduit for upper‑limb arterial flow
Landmark for cuff blood pressure measurement

sections.p: It runs in the medial bicipital groove, initially lateral to the biceps tendon, then crosses medially at the mid‑arm. It is a thick, pulsatile vessel with a muscular wall.
In the arm the brachial artery is accompanied laterally by the median nerve and deep by the profunda brachii artery; the radial nerve crosses it near the lateral epicondyle.
b: Distal: radial nerve at cubital fossa

sections.p: It receives blood from the axillary artery and gives off several branches that nourish the arm muscles and skin.
b: Superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries

sections.p: The arterial wall is innervated by sympathetic fibers traveling with the adjacent nerves, influencing vasomotor tone.
b: Sympathetic fibers via the brachial plexus

sections.p: Delivers oxygenated blood to the elbow, forearm, and hand; provides a palpable pulse for clinical assessment and a site for arterial cannulation.
b: Access for arterial line in critical care

sections.p: Trauma, thrombosis, or iatrogenic injury can compromise limb perfusion. The artery is also a common site for aneurysm formation in patients with connective‑tissue disease or infection.
b: Aneurysm → pulsatile mass, risk of rupture

t.b: Is there flow obstruction? → Absent or dampened flow confirms thrombosis or severe stenosis
Is perfusion adequate? → Ratio <0.9 suggests significant arterial disease
What is the anatomy of a suspected aneurysm? → Shows size, neck, and relation to nerves; if unavailable, use bedside Doppler

sections.p: Know the landmarks for palpation, the sequence of blood pressure measurement, and how to recognize vascular compromise in the arm.
b: Pulse felt 1–2 cm medial to biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa
Cuff lower edge 2–3 cm above elbow crease for accurate BP

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of pulse or cold, pale hand → acute arterial occlusion
Rapidly expanding forearm swelling after trauma → possible pseudoaneurysm or compartment syndrome
Severe pain with absent distal pulses → limb‑threatening ischemia

faq.q: Why is the brachial artery used for blood pressure measurement?
faq.a: Because it is superficial, has a strong pulse, and reflects central arterial pressure accurately.

faq.q: What is the difference between a true aneurysm and a pseudoaneurysm of the brachial artery?
faq.a: A true aneurysm involves all vessel wall layers; a pseudoaneurysm is a contained rupture with blood outside the wall.

faq.q: How can you differentiate brachial artery thrombosis from a nerve injury?
faq.a: Thrombosis causes loss of pulse and coldness; nerve injury causes motor/sensory loss without vascular signs.

exam: Identify the brachial artery on a diagram of the arm and name its major branches.
Explain how cuff placement affects systolic and diastolic blood pressure readings.
Describe the clinical signs of acute brachial artery occlusion and immediate management steps.
